item.title: The Dog That Was Wagged: Jason Arday — J’Accuse Rusbridger and Barber

item.content:encoded:
Towards the end of their forty-five-minute Media Confidential conversation about the life and death of Professor Jason Arday, the former editors Lionel Barber and Alan Rusbridger at last arrive at the question of what lessons might be learned. Rusbridger thinks the debate should be held within the media rather than on social media, because social media is not a very good place for such a debate. But that, Alan, is precisely the point. Social media may be a very bad place to debate the conduct of journalists, but it is now the place where journalists discover, select, test and intensify the subjects of their journalism.

The reporters at your former newspaper were not standing outside this degraded conversation, looking in through the plate glass of their professional standards: they were in it, receiving its signals, adding their own, watching the reaction to what they had added and converting that reaction into the warrant for further publication. Social media was not the vulgar aftermath of the Jason Arday story: it was the tail that wagged this particular dog, just as it has so many others since the advent of bi-directional digital media–in the form of the mobile phone and wireless broadband–over twenty years ago. Look, I know you fellows are getting a little long in the tooth, but you have heard of mobile phones, haven’t you? Possibly even of teeth going blue? I cannot imagine it took your grandfathers from 1908 until 1930 to assimilate the fact that aeroplanes were now in the sky.

So why is it taking you so long to appreciate what bidirectionality implies for the media? You, Alan, are Cambridge-educated, while Lionel is an Oxford man; and as seasoned media professionals you might conceivably have dipped into Marshall McLuhan’s ‘Understanding Media’. I’m not suggesting you would have read the whole thing–John Junor forefend!–but you might at least have ventured beyond the bald statement that ‘the medium is the message’, and attempted to understand the relationship between content and the means by which it is mediated. You are journalists, after all. Or are you now something else altogether–podcasters, perhaps? You must be aware that listening and reading involve different kinds of attention and retention; and that the metrics governing what people absorb online have themselves become part of the way news is selected and structured. Yet you show no awareness of any of this.

Listening to your podcast, I could almost hear the rattle of a freshly ironed copy of the Daily Telegraph as it was fitted to a wooden reading stick and hung on the rack of some Pall Mall gentlemen’s club. The largest story in the media world you describe might still be Phileas Fogg going around the world in eighty days. But, gentlemen, that ship has sailed. Media now circumnavigates the world in eighty-thousandths of a second. Still, I’ve retained a fair bit of your conversation–and it ranged pretty widely: Race is present from the beginning–autism is not. Almost twenty-seven minutes of a forty-five-minute broadcast elapse before the fact that the man whose treatment they are examining was autistic is allowed any real conceptual weight. Warnings are mentioned, but aggregated in such a way as to dissolve their force. An Andrew Neil tweet expressing concern about Arday’s mental health becomes one item in a miscellany.

Simon Baron-Cohen’s intervention is acknowledged, but not his standing: he is not simply a kindly Cambridge colleague who asked Fleet Street to ease off, but the director of Cambridge’s Autism Research Centre, a pioneer of large-scale research into suicidality among autistic people, and a man making an explicit safeguarding intervention: ‘This is relentless bullying of a vulnerable autistic man and raises safeguarding issues. It’s time to stop.’ I’ve spoken to Professor Sir Simon Baron-Cohen on this matter, as he happens to be a childhood friend of mine. Perhaps The Guardian should send a reporter to check up on this and ask how I know that he is, in fact, an expert in suicidality among autistic people? I doubt such reporting will provoke suicide in Simon himself, but I’m sure it will contribute to his distress as he mourns a personal friend, a disabled man he warned the media to leave alone, Alan and Lionel.

As for the fact that the Guardian’s newsroom was directly warned about Jason Arday’s mental health, this was not mentioned at all by the garrulous old chums. I’ll remind them: an email was sent to the editor, Katharine Viner, explicitly asking for coverage to be toned down. It was replied to by the Head of News, Archie Bland, who said that he saw no reason to do so. Why was this not part of your conversation? Given that you want to keep that debate within the media itself. This omission of any serious understanding or consideration of Arday being autistic is shocking. I write as the parent of two diagnosed autistic people and I have a third neurodivergent child. The ableism running through the Barber–Rusbridger discussion is not only a failure to use the approved vocabulary.

It’s the far graver evidence of unwillingness to even attempt to understand what autism is, how it may bear upon literalness, perseveration, shame, psychic overwhelm and suicidality, and why the usual newsroom distinction between a person’s ‘mental health’ and the legitimate public examination of his conduct may be lethally inadequate. Arday’s autism was not a picturesque feature of the inspirational story his universities had helped to manufacture, and as we can see, it was far from being an immunity card: it was a diagnosed condition that ought to have changed the manner, tempo and proportionality of the reporting. Journalists who chose to write repeatedly about an autistic man had an obligation to learn what they were writing about. Listening to Rusbridger and Barber, I was reminded of Private Eye’s Lunchtime O’Booze and his mental health problems.

Barber and Rusbridger aren’t so O’Booze that they can’t acknowledge that the story became excessive. They discuss the Cofnas and right-wing axis and are rightly contemptuous of those who treated Arday as the spoil in a war against diversity, equity and inclusion. Yet the moral axis they draw is chiefly the familiar one between publications and political tendencies they approve of and those they do not. Bad newspapers and right-wing ideologues (Lord Young of X, see SITREP passim) behaved badly; serious liberal journalism, by implication, supplied nuance. The effect is to preserve the innocence of their own caste, and once again you hear that yellowing broadsheet being ironed by a flunkey. Guardian News & Media has said that its reporting followed ‘months of careful review’, that its commentary was ‘nuanced and balanced’, and that ‘we stand by our journalists’.

All three propositions may be true of individual texts and still fail to answer the accusation. Metrics measure attention, not morality; nuance is not an antidote to accumulation; balance within one article cannot acquit a sequence of articles whose effects become inputs into the next act of publication. I’m not questioning if each brick met the building regulations–it’s what the bricks built. The Guardian’s institutional line runs through actual editors sitting at actual desks: from its reporters and commissioning editors to Archie Bland, Katharine Viner, Guardian News & Media and, ultimately, the Scott Trust chaired by Ole Jacob Sunde. The Trust exists to secure the Guardian’s editorial and financial independence, and its shareholders take no dividend. That makes the newspaper different from the Telegraph, Mail, Times or Sun.

However, it does not place it outside the attention economy: a publication dependent on scale, reader loyalty, contributions and digital engagement is exposed to the same command, even when no proprietor extracts the resulting surplus. That command is MORE: more items, more users, more reaction, more duration, more recursion. At a proprietorial newspaper MORE terminates in shareholder value. At the Guardian it may terminate in the preservation of the institution and its liberal mission in the form of its editors and former editors’ reputations, rather than their reality. Ole Jacob Sunde was brought on to the Scott Trust in 2015, and made its chair in 2021, precisely because of his experience in leading legacy media into the digital age. For two decades he chaired Schibsted, the Scandinavian media group that carried its old news businesses online while creating immense value through digital marketplaces and services.

When Sunde was appointed, David Olusoga explicitly cited his ‘deep expertise in digital media’. So The Guardian cannot plausibly present itself as some venerable print institution accidentally ambushed by the internet and its queered mediatising problematic: its governing body understood perfectly well that it was becoming a major node in international digital-media networks. Besides, The Guardian had already gone belly-up to the web under Rusbridger. It nobly sucked up the boosters’ ‘digital democracy’ hype, rejected the paywall and seemed at times to imagine itself as some new incarnation of the Whole Earth Catalog, rather than a venerable British newspaper entering into dependency upon search engines, platforms and measurable attention.

Twenty years later it wears a print mask, from behind which you can see the Google Glass sinisterly glittering; and it is behind that glass that the people its journalists write about are converted into digestible content. Trust me, Alan: whether the teeth belong to a Guardian reporter or to someone at The Times—which you lambast for using Arday’s death to flog its rag—they feel much the same to the person between them. The only teeth Rusbridger and Barber appear to fear are those of lawyers and potential press regulators–this tends to be because of the residual omerta on Fleet Street that allows powerful people in the media to escape media attention. I wonder how they would like their own former journalists poking zealously into their lives? Neither of them would be free of scandal if they were subjected to the same level of scrutiny as Arday, because NO ONE would.

Yet these invulnerables talk as though the publications they have edited constitute the only possible means by which the governed can discover the truth about their governors. Even setting to one side the fact that they are both fully paid up establishmentarians, it needs stressing that some of the defining investigations of the past twenty years have originated outside traditional Fleet Street structures, or have depended upon whistleblowers, non-profit organisations, international collaborations and distributed digital research networks. More importantly, many of the stories that now require investigation concern corporate systems in which legacy media organisations are themselves commercially and technologically embedded.

The only D notice that Churchill imposed during the early years of the Second World War was to forbid the press to report the desertions of men who had returned from Dunkirk disgusted with the behaviour of their officers. I notice the same sort of tendency in the British media itself: a Churchillian desire to avoid the shame of defeat. However, nobody has imposed a D notice on me. So, here we have two men denying the need for their profession to submit to genuinely independent regulation while speaking on behalf of institutions dependent upon companies whose objectives may be altogether different from those espoused in newspaper editorials. The old freedom-of-the-press argument presumed that the newspaper stood between concentrated power and the public. But what happens when the newspaper is itself operationally nested inside concentrations of power far greater than anything dear old C. P. Scott could have imagined?

(And that was long before GNM’s ownership of Autotrader and its subsequent sale allowed them to effectively convert the buying and selling of the nation’s Vauxhall Astras into the sword of truth and justice they allegedly wield.) But if it ain’t Al and Leo, who then is afflicting the comfortable–and who is merely servicing their content? The old maxim is indeed that the newspaper should comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable. Barber and Rusbridger are very comfortable men: this is not an insult but a material fact about their position in the British establishment.

As two former editors able to discuss the culpability of newspapers from within the protective afterlife of successful editorial careers, the comfort they are least willing to afflict is not simply that of shareholders, it’s rather the professional comfort of believing that journalism remains a sovereign activity: the editor acts upon ‘the news’ and produces a representation of reality for the reader. To hear them discuss this process of debating culpability ‘within the media’ was particularly jarring for me, given my own experiences. Rusbridger is now an editor-at-large at The New World, formerly The New European. He did not join the paper until 2026, so bears no responsibility for what follows; but the institution provides a useful specimen of the deliberation he recommends.

In September 2024, while I was a columnist there, I submitted a satire about A$AP Rocky, Bottega Veneta, rap, luxury consumption and the Hegelian master–slave dialectic. Its argument was that the folie à deux between luxury brands and African-American rap stars converts racial rebellion into conspicuous consumption, while liberal fear of appearing racist disables criticism of the violence and misogyny marketed with it. The editor, Steve Anglesey, rejected it because he was ‘not interested in publishing something that’s going to see you and us called racists’; declared the decision final; refused further discussion; and invited a replacement column. When I objected to being tried for prospective racism without so much as a conversation–and pointed out that I had had the piece read and approved by two Black colleagues–the publisher, Matt Kelly, replied: ‘Fucking grow up.’ The column, he said, was ‘unintelligible, self-indulgent bullshit’.

(You may be the judge of that: I still stand by it, and will post it immediately after this one.) He also refused to speak to me on the telephone. The partnership was over: more than half a decade during which I had produced hundreds of articles for them and written an entire Brexit edition of the newspaper single-handedly. I scarcely need to adduce further evidence of their understanding of safeguarding–in this instance, the safeguarding of one of their own journalists rather than of the subject of one–but nonetheless I will. A fortnight after this exchange with two venerable legacy journalists, who had debated my piece in so measured and nuanced a manner–‘nuanced’ being a word Lionel and Alan particularly enjoy deploying when discussing journalism–I entered hospital for an allogeneic stem-cell transplant necessitated by secondary myelofibrosis: a medical procedure carrying a one-in-five chance of death. Were my editors aware of this?

You bet your fucking arse they were. Oops. Perhaps I shouldn’t say that… Oh yes I can. I’m not writing for The Guardian anymore, or the piss-poor New World for that matter. An editor is entitled to reject a column–he’s also entitled to think its argument wrong, reckless or repellent. What is revealing–besides the almost unbelievable callousness and, frankly, ingratitude–is the substitution of anticipated social-media accusations–‘going to see you and us called racists’–for editorial judgement, and then the refusal of the internal debate supposedly superior to the online one. The dog pre-emptively wagged itself in expectation of the tail. A newspaper protected its reputation from an imagined digital reaction by suppressing an argument about the very racial inhibitions producing that reaction, while two senior editors reserved to themselves both the verdict and the right not to explain it.

If this is what keeping the debate ‘within the media’ means, the phrase denotes not a forum but a locked room. Of course, Anglesey and Kelly may also have been responding to a demand I had made a week or two earlier: that the Martin Rowson byline drawing accompanying my column be removed, and that he no longer be commissioned to illustrate any of my work. Why? Because Rowson had produced a cartoon condemned as antisemitic–subsequently withdrawn and apologised for–in, you guessed it, The Guardian. I no longer wished to be associated with someone whose published work had made him, in that instance, a de facto racist. You couldn’t, as the late John Junor would have said, make it up. Setting aside personal history, the significant point is that bi-directional digital media completely abolished the crude Cartesianism of these two press philosophes.

Publication now decisively alters the field it purports to describe: an article produces searches, posts, denunciations, defences and fresh disclosures; those reactions are counted; the counts enter editorial judgement; that judgement produces another article. Reality is recursively reordered around the journalist writing the story. The public interest becomes indistinguishable from the public being interested, while the measurable fact of interest is used as evidence that further publication serves the public. I said all of this in my last SITREP, but while the dynamic old duo namechecked it, they didn’t, duh, really seem to have read it. Too busy doom-scrolling, sans doute. This is where search-engine optimisation matters–and not just for pornography preferences or Googling yourself.

There are two possibilities, and both may well have been operating at once: it’s exactly evidence of this that any responsible inquiry would have to look for. A journalist or sub-editor may consciously fashion a headline around the terms most likely to obtain search traffic and generate distinct URLs: there may well have been conferences, informal meetings, and even online exhortations to ensure precisely this by putting terms such as ‘Black’, ‘plagiarist’, ‘Cambridge’ etc in the same headlines and subheads. Or, nobody need consciously decide to persecute anybody: the publishing system rewards the language, timing and multiplication of items that produce discoverability, and gradually entrains its users–the ‘users’ being both hacks and who they’re hacking away at. The first phenomenon is intentional in the ordinary sense, the second is distributed pseudo-intentionality.

But the important point is that the latter does not absolve the former. The NewsCord count gives the process a crude silhouette: after Cambridge announced a new inquiry, 249 articles appeared over twenty-two days; 188 more followed Arday’s resignation and his statement that he had ‘reached the limit of what any person could reasonably endure’. These numbers do not prove that SEO–search-engine optimisation–killed a man. They show the conversion of an institutional event into renewable media inventory, and of expressed distress into a further news peg. As I’ve iterated before and must now sadly reiterate: they hurt him; people watched; they saw people watching; they hurt him again. Everyone was only responding–nobody was responsible. But somebody wrote every word; somebody commissioned every article; somebody pressed publish.

It’s against this tawdry blurry background that we have to consider the limited ‘mea culpas’ issued by journalists and commentators whose interventions contributed to the persecution of a Black autistic man in the weeks preceding his death. Aaron Bastani’s was the most unequivocal: having dismissed Arday as a ‘conman’ and described one of his lectures as saying ‘nothing’, Bastani subsequently said: ‘I’m sorry, I apologise. Journalism is when you seek the facts. It’s a quest for the truth … This was anything but. It was bile. It’s everything I dislike about the modern media.’ He added that an apology was insufficient; that he wished he could ask Arday’s forgiveness; and that he had ‘really screwed up’. This is honourable as far as it goes–and it goes considerably further than most.

But it still construes the offence primarily as a personal ethical lapse: Bastani said something cruel; Bastani repents; Bastani wishes he could obtain absolution from the dead man. What remains unexamined is how his bile was solicited, circulated and operationalised by the same media system he claims to dislike. His mistake was that his status, platform, followers and facility for the contemptuous capsule made his high-octane bile available as fuel for everybody else’s. Matthew Syed’s confession was more complex: in a column entitled ‘Jason Arday was failed by the system–and by me’, he admitted that, while the attacks intensified, a friend had urged him to defend Arday; that he had prevaricated in ways he now considered cowardly; and that he had failed to say publicly that legitimate criticism had become disproportionate and dangerous.

Again, this deserves acknowledgement: Syed at least understands that culpability may consist not only in joining the attack but in withholding resistance when one has the authority to make it consequential. However his confession contains such a gaping lacuna that were I on the other side of the grille I’d certainly refuse absolution: What was he afraid of? Whose displeasure did he anticipate? Syed is a highly successful Times columnist, scarcely a precarious junior reporter: his media company has disclosed more than two million pounds in net assets, while his bestselling books, corporate consultancy and five-figure speaking engagements make him, by any reasonable definition, a very comfortable man. What, precisely, did a journalist with such material and professional insulation imagine he had to lose?

Why did he feel unable to protest, within a newspaper publishing article after article about Arday, that the cumulative process had become dangerous? Syed locates cowardice in himself while leaving the machinery that produced his fear largely undescribed. The call was coming from inside the house–but apparently the house itself must remain offstage, and the phone, anyway, was off the hook. Tim Stanley also deserves qualified commendation. Before Arday’s death he had participated with Jacob Rees-Mogg in a Telegraph discussion of the supposed downfall of Cambridge’s ‘woke poster boy’. When I wrote to Stanley afterwards and asked him to consider what he knew about the editorial coordination of the coverage–and, in effect, whether his conscience required him to rat out his colleagues–he replied courteously, although he declined to do so.

That is better than silence and infinitely better than abuse; however, it leaves fully intact the Fleet Street omertà whereby journalists demand transparency from every other institution while treating their own editorial conferences as inviolable mysteries. Conscience is permitted among Catholics such as Stanley and Rees-Mogg in their podcast confessional, but disclosure to the rest of the congregation is emphatically not. These are the penitents, then, but they’re hardly in sackcloth and ashes: one who confesses cruelty without comprehending its logistical amplification; one who confesses cowardice without naming the institution that frightened him; and one who will discuss conscience but not colleagues. I commend all three for feeling guilt–guilt is at least evidence that some moral sensation persists.

But none appears to understand exactly what he is guilty of, because each continues to imagine his action or inaction as an autonomous item rather than as one relay in a recursive system: this makes amends altogether surplus to its requirements, and consequently to their own. I will dig into them: the effect of publication became an input into the next act of publication. Their guilt is distributed because their agency was distributed—but distributed agency distributes responsibility; it does not abolish it. Across what used to be an aisle, but will soon enough if things carry on become a river of blood, sit those who have declined even this inadequate reckoning. Sarah Ditum wrote after Arday’s death that the press did not kill him; she did ‘not regret writing about Arday’, although she was sorry for him and ‘for all of us’ that he had been placed in such a position.

I’m sorry for her, too, with reasoning like that she must take several attempts to get through a door. Her defence is a befittingly hackneyed one: the allegations were newsworthy; the subject occupied a senior post at an elite university; journalists were doing their jobs. But nobody seriously has argued that the plagiarism allegations should never have been investigated–the accusation concerns scale, tone, sequencing, ridicule and the conversion of each reaction into permission for another attack. ‘I was doing my job’ answers the question of occupational identity while evading the question of cumulative effect. It also, Sarah, has obvious overtones of ‘I was only following orders.’ Orders that in this case, you didn’t even know the issuer of.

Julia Hartley-Brewer went further, responding after Arday’s death with the sort of posthumous derision that confirms the incapacity of ideological certainty to recognise a corpse as the terminus of an argument: she really would be in good company with Ku Klux Klan members who’d just lynched a Black person. Others on the right repeated that Arday alone was responsible for his death; that he had been a liar and fraud rightly exposed; that any suggestion of media culpability was emotional blackmail directed against–Oh! The horror!–journalism. The logic is immaculate because it is circular: the coverage was justified because Arday was guilty, and Arday’s guilt is demonstrated by the volume and confidence of the coverage. The persecution proves the offence for which persecution was required: it’s called a diallelus in reasoning, or a circular argument.

I’m not surprised these people deploy it, their only justification for anything at all is that they feel so very… justified. At the institutional-liberal end of the round-robin, The Guardian performed an apparently contrary but structurally identical manoeuvre. Its statement, as I’ve written above, asserted that its journalism had followed ‘months of careful review’, had been ‘nuanced and balanced’, and that it stood by its journalists. It then foregrounded the racialised social-media abuse suffered by Black reporters involved in the coverage. Such abuse is vile and should be condemned without qualification–however, its existence cannot function as retrospective absolution for the journalism itself. The fact that reporters were abused does not establish that their reporting was proportionate; any more than legitimate reporting of Arday’s possible misconduct established that every subsequent item was necessary.

Vulnerability is not a transferable moral credit–and the suffering of journalists cannot be used to cancel the suffering of their subject. So the right predictably doubles down because it cannot admit that an anti-DEI crusade, started by a racist and fomented by them, became a hunt. While the liberal press doubles down because it cannot admit that ‘nuanced and balanced’ articles may aggregate into persecution. So the few penitents beat their tits without examining the media physiology that made the tit-beating necessary. Everybody gets their corpus callosums in a twist, such that the hemispheres reverse themselves, and the right, supposedly devoted to individual responsibility, discovers distributed innocence for journalists acting collectively; the liberal left, supposedly alert to structural power, insists upon judging every article as an isolated individual act.

And this, Alan me old mucker, is the debate you wish to keep ‘within the media’. It consists of journalists recommitting themselves to their previous ideological positions–‘I am not a racist. I was only reporting. I was pursuing truth. I stand by my colleagues’.–or issuing apologies that preserve the fiction of autonomous professional agency. You and Leo preside over this dream of reality as though the old categories still corresponded to the mechanism: legitimate or illegitimate journalism, left or right, racist or anti-racist, careful reporting or social-media abuse. Meanwhile the recursive machine runs through every category and converts each defence, accusation, apology and counter-accusation into further inventory.

What the spectacle resembles overall is a little intramural tit-beating ceremony: Fleet Street thumping its own collective chest–sometimes penitentially, sometimes defiantly–almost as though this professional timpani might drown out the noise of public disgust. But the public can hear perfectly well–more importantly, it can see. It has watched journalism investigate everybody except itself, comfort its own afflicted and afflict anybody made sufficiently interesting by the metrics. You call this a debate? It’s the muffled snoring of a tired old industry dreaming that it is awake and chasing the evil rabbits of some forgotten era. My dear dead Jack Russell, when he got hold of anything–a stick, a slipper, a newspaper–would shake it as if his little life depended upon killing it. The British legacy media now resembles the object in the animal’s jaws.

The vicious little Jack Russell shaking it is social media–but social media is itself clamped in the jaws of a far larger dog: the magnificent seven technology companies and their stupendous market capitalisations, shaking the platforms for more churn, more arousal, more behavioural data and more capital return. Each dog experiences the convulsions transmitted through it as its own activity. Each imagines it has chosen to do the shaking, while completely failing to notice how it’s being… shaken. This is the Brocken spectre of contemporary modernity: a pseudo-intentional, recursive and distributed logistical system, magnified by the vapours through which we project it, which appears to possess a single malevolent will although it is constituted by countless situated acts. There need be no conspiracy.

The system can produce the phenomenology of concerted persecution out of competition, imitation, metrics, ideology, institutional cowardice and the ordinary libidinal pleasure of joining in good old ‘pile on’. Paul Tiyambe Zeleza approaches the other side of this apparatus in his powerful Substack essay, Who Killed Jason Arday? Zeleza, a Malawian-born historian, Africanist and former vice-chancellor with experience of both American and British higher education, is exceptionally well placed to describe the institutional manufacture of exemplary Black achievement. His formulation is devastating: Arday was eagerly elevated as a symbol, ruthlessly scrutinised as an anomaly and callously discarded as a liability. Cambridge made capital from the story of the youngest Black professor in its history; the story joined autism, late speech, poverty and apparently superhuman feats of endurance into an institutional allegory of transformation.

When the allegory became reputationally expensive, the institution announced another inquiry. Zeleza correctly arraigns the actors whom Barber and Rusbridger treat more abstractly: universities that substitute symbolic appointments for structural change; administrators who turn biography into branding; appointment and vetting systems that borrow the lustre of exceptional lives and then disclaim responsibility for having burnished them. His essay should be read. But his title also poses the difficulty. Who killed Jason Arday? invites the restoration of a sovereign intending subject at precisely the point where causation has become distributed. Even an account as institutionally sophisticated as Zeleza’s tends to allot intention to entities–Cambridge, DEI, the liberal university–which are themselves being operationalised by digital systems of recruitment, assessment, publicity, ranking and risk.

The sequence matters: Liverpool John Moores University had already investigated the plagiarism allegations and did not find Arday guilty of research misconduct. Cambridge later announced a fresh inquiry after receiving what it described as new information. I contend that the announcement was not a neutral administrative punctuation mark, because it changed the status of every allegation in the media field. Cambridge itself effectively licensed republication and supplied a fresh URL. It made the old material new, and the speculative material reportable. When Arday resigned, Cambridge had dropped the soon-to-be-dead donkey while retaining the posture of procedural rectitude. Whether or not that was anyone’s conscious intention, it was the institutional effect. At the Cambridge vigil, the university’s vice-chancellor, Deborah Prentice, was heckled and jostled while attempting to speak.

That event, too, belongs in the sequence–not because intimidation should be romanticised, but because it showed the university’s attempt to remain the neutral custodian of a tragedy it had helped to structure was no longer credible to the crowd. Barber and Rusbridger discuss Cambridge’s DEI policies in generalities, they spoke of the rigorousness of academic panels they themselves had sat on, but they did not reconstruct the relay: appointment, promotion, publicity, allegation, prior inquiry, new inquiry, multiplying coverage, resignation, death, institutional condolence. Without the relay there is no causation, only opinion. British universities are not standing outside the digital transformation any more than British newspapers are. Why? Because they inhabit the same Potemkin village. It’s a funny old village, what with its ramifying institutions, the nameplates of which still say scholarship, judgement, tutorial, collegium.

Funny peculiar though, not ha-ha, because behind them operates a transactional machinery of online recruitment, clearing targets, league tables, student-satisfaction scores, electronic submission, plagiarism reports, digital marking, moderation trails, appeals, deferrals and retention metrics. In my fourteen years teaching in a British university, I was never permitted simply to fail a student whose work I believed had failed. I saw an essay containing twenty-seven per cent matched material survive the very plagiarism machinery ostensibly designed to guarantee probity. Arts and humanities students could pass terms while ‘writing’ two two-thousand-word essays and reading a pitiful number of books. Academics were sent on recruitment drives to China and India; departments watched recruitment figures arranged as competitive tables. As overseas demand weakened, the pressure to recruit and retain intensified.

Digital assessment does not by itself inflate grades, any more than a search box writes a persecutory headline. However, it does render academic work continuously measurable, reproducible, comparable, appealable and administratively visible. It makes every exercise of judgement an entry in a system whose other imperatives are recruitment, retention and customer satisfaction. In England, the proportion of first-class degrees rose from 15.5 per cent in 2010–11 to 32.8 per cent in 2021–22. The Office for Students calculated that half of those Firsts could not be explained by observable changes including entry qualifications and subject mix. The peak was intensified by the pandemic and has since fallen, but the level remains far above the earlier baseline. The curve establishes grade inflation. It does not, in and of itself, establish digitisation as the cause.

The causal claim is visible in the institutional circuitry: digital systems make the resistance of an individual examiner legible as friction and enable that friction to be managed away. The young journalists entering newsrooms have themselves passed through this transformed university. Many have read fewer whole books, written fewer sustained essays and become more practised in the manipulation of searchable fragments. Their senior editors have children who have passed through it–despite that, Rusbridger says he is not qualified to judge the seriousness of the plagiarism alleged against Arday, he treats the question as a technical mystery. It is not.

One can hold simultaneously that plagiarism matters and that Arday’s work deserved proper scrutiny and that Liverpool John Moores had not found him guilty of misconduct and that Cambridge was entitled to examine genuinely new evidence and that the public multiplication of accusations against a vulnerable autistic man became grotesquely disproportionate. What the digital university and the digital newsroom share is their preference for the similarity score, the count, the rank and the procedural audit over difficult acts of situated judgement. Try reading Emile Durkheim on suicide, Alan, it’s all you, personally, need to know about sociology in order to judge the media’s treatment of vulnerable Black autistic man. You do have a Cambridge degree in English Literature after all, just like Oor Andy. But neither of you are literary types, really, which is just as well given the British literary world participates in the same pretence.

Newspapers, universities and publishing houses retain their historic names, buildings, hierarchies and rituals, as if gyroscopically mounted to preserve their old equilibrium while the world rotates violently around them. Journalists continue to speak as if they report upon a reality independent of their reports. Academics continue to speak as if they assess work independent of the systems through which it is submitted, checked, ranked and monetised. And editors continue to defend each item separately when the accusation concerns the recursive whole. This is why Rusbridger’s closing wish–to keep the debate within the media and away from social media–is so perfectly, terribly wrong. There is no longer any ‘within the media’ that excludes social media.

Nor is there a university outside the digital marketplace, or a Guardian outside the attention economy, or an autistic subject outside the networked gaze that made his life simultaneously inspirational copy, ideological evidence, searchable allegation and spectacle. The first task is for Oor Andy to stop eating chips, unrumple the old newsprint they’re wrapped in, and ironing it properly in the form of an independent public inquiry capable of examining the whole causal chain: university governance and appointment; the sequencing of Cambridge’s decisions; newsroom knowledge of Arday’s autism and the safeguarding warnings; editorial commissioning; headline construction and SEO; traffic and engagement data; the transmission of material between social and legacy media; and the adequacy of IPSO and internal complaints procedures.

Barber and Rusbridger are resistant to statutory intervention, political involvement and even meaningful scrutiny by a genuinely independent regulator. But a profession cannot claim the right to investigate every other institution while reserving the investigation of itself to conversations among its retired commanders. The second task is moral rather than procedural. Journalists must recover the experience of discomfort: not the performative discomfort of confessing that ‘the media’ went too far, but the intimate discomfort of asking what one’s own article did after it left one’s hands. Then what the next journalist did with its effects, what warning was received and discounted, what vulnerability was known, what pleasure was taken in the chase, and finally what institutional interest was served by calling each new convulsion news.

Jason Arday was converted into an object of distributed regard: race helped select the object—ableism helped make his vulnerability illegible. Universities inflated the symbolic figure and then protected themselves from its collapse. Legacy journalism did what it does best nowadays: supplying the authority that produces much, much more repetition. Social media may well have supplied velocity, appetite and apparent public warrant, but the same platforms that support the entire legacy media supplied the architecture of recurrence. And most importantly, it’s capital–which knows no borders, allegiances and disabilities, while recognising vulnerabilities only to then exploit them–that supplied the command: MORE. No one dog needs to have intended the killing, but the thing in their jaws is dead.

All they can do is cast around for somewhere to bury it, before walking off in that slightly embarrassed way that dogs do when they’ve just done a big, bad shit.
